prompt: A client says they run "LeSS" with five teams. Mark the practices that are not LeSS.

task.prompt: A client says they run "LeSS" with five teams. Mark the practices that are not LeSS.

segments.text: One Product Owner and one Product Backlog for the whole product.
Each team has its own Product Owner and backlog.
segments.issue: LeSS has one Product Owner and one Product Backlog across all teams.

segments.text: All teams share one Sprint and produce one integrated increment.
Teams are organised as component teams: API team, iOS team, web team.
segments.issue: LeSS prefers cross-functional feature teams; component teams create cross-team handoffs.

segments.text: Sprint Planning has two parts: a shared Part 1 and team-level Part 2.
There is an overall retrospective after the team retrospectives.
Each team picks its own sprint length.
segments.issue: All teams in LeSS work in one common Sprint.

segments.text: Teams coordinate directly, e.g. by talking or joint refinement.

prompt: Order these Nexus events within a Sprint.

task.prompt: Order these Nexus events within a Sprint.

items.label: Nexus Daily Scrum, then team Daily Scrums

task.explanation: Nexus wraps Scrum events with a Nexus-level version: plan together, sync daily on integration, review one integrated increment, then improve together.

prompt: A client with four Scrum teams on one product asks how to coordinate better. Integration issues surface late, and each team optimises its own sprint.

task.prompt: A client with four Scrum teams on one product asks how to coordinate better. Integration issues surface late, and each team optimises its own sprint.

steps.question: Which response fits best?
options: Give each team a separate product to own
Introduce a lightweight scaling approach such as Nexus or LeSS: one backlog, a shared Sprint, and an integrated increment each Sprint
Add a separate integration phase at the end
Increase the number of status meetings
steps.explanation: These frameworks address exactly late integration and local optimisation.

steps.question: In Nexus, who is accountable for resolving integration issues?
options: The Nexus Integration Team
Each team's developers separately
The client's CTO
The Scrum of Scrums chair
steps.explanation: Nexus adds a Nexus Integration Team accountable for an integrated increment.

prompt: Order these from the least to the most structure added on top of plain Scrum.

task.prompt: Order these from the least to the most structure added on top of plain Scrum.

items.label: A Scrum of Scrums meeting between team representatives
LeSS: one backlog, one Product Owner and a shared Sprint for all teams
SAFe: Agile Release Trains, extra roles, and solution and portfolio layers

task.explanation: A Scrum of Scrums is only a coordination meeting; LeSS is Scrum applied to many teams with minimal additions; SAFe adds roles, events and whole management layers.

prompt: Oyelabs and another agency each have one team working on the same client product. Their sprints are on different schedules.

task.prompt: Oyelabs and another agency each have one team working on the same client product. Their sprints are on different schedules.

steps.question: What is the simplest helpful change?
options: Align sprint cadences and hold a short Scrum of Scrums with joint refinement for shared items
Adopt SAFe
Merge the agencies
Integrate only before launch
steps.explanation: Two teams need light coordination, not a heavy framework.

steps.question: What artefact helps most?
options: Separate backlogs with no link
A Gantt chart per agency
A weekly email of finished tickets
One shared, ordered backlog for the product with cross-team dependencies visible

prompt: Basic LeSS is designed for up to about eight teams. A client has 60 developers on one product and wants teams of about 7.

task.prompt: Basic LeSS is designed for up to about eight teams. A client has 60 developers on one product and wants teams of about 7.

fields.label: Teams above the Basic LeSS limit

task.explanation: 60 / 7 = 8.6, so 9 teams; that is beyond Basic LeSS, so LeSS Huge (requirement areas) or fewer, larger teams would apply.

prompt: What does LeSS Huge add for very large products?

options: A separate backlog per team
A portfolio layer with lean budgets
Requirement areas, each with an Area Product Owner, under one overall Product Owner
A Release Train Engineer
mcq.explanation: LeSS Huge keeps one product and one backlog, grouped into requirement areas.

prompt: What is a Scrum of Scrums?

options: A framework with its own roles and certification
A sprint containing several smaller sprints
A retrospective about other retrospectives
A meeting where representatives from several teams coordinate dependencies and impediments
mcq.explanation: It is a coordination technique, not a full scaling framework.

prompt: Why do LeSS and Nexus favour feature teams over component teams?

options: Feature teams can deliver end-to-end value, reducing cross-team handoffs and integration delays
Component teams are cheaper
Feature teams need no Product Owner
Feature teams never integrate
mcq.explanation: Component teams turn every feature into a dependency chain.
